en: The Laghu-mādhyandinīya Śikṣā:
Now I shall proclaim the Śikṣā according to the doctrine of Mādhyandina: that the letter *ś* should become *kh* when followed by *t*, but this does not occur when there is a conjunction with *u*. (1)

In the word *iṣe*, *lakṣyam* [is the example]; *kṛṣṇa-ukṣā* and *samudraḥ* are the counter-examples (*pratyudāhṛti*). For when a letter standing at the beginning of a word is not joined [with another], and for which the substitute *ja* occurs—provided it is joined by means of elision (*haraṇa*)—[the rule applies].
By means of sacrifice, one perceives the sacrifice; this is illustrated by the example of the peacock (*mayūra*).
Therefore, from that which is known as the "all-sacrificed" (*sarvahuta*), and likewise from that very source, it shall in every way consist of the letter *ra* joined with the letter *ha*. 3–4.
The sun is external; however, for the sake of *śaṣpyā*, there is a counter-example. In every case, the letter *ja* occurs when joined with the letters *ya* and *ra*.
Likewise, it does not occur after a prefix when joined with *saharayyā* or *vyṛddhyā*.

It is cited as an example that [the syllable] *ya* is used even among humans when it is joined with a preceding vowel (*upayajñam*). The letter *va* should be known as a "heavy" (*guru*) syllable when it occurs at the beginning of a word;
*vibhrāṭ* is cited as an example, while *savitā* is recorded as having a short vowel in its interior (*antarlaghu*).
At the end of a word, *vāyu* and *ṛtaspate* are indeed very light;
however, when followed by a prefix, the letter *s* is considered light. In the recitation of mantras, *vo*, *vām*, and *vai* are light within a word, but heavy at the end of a word.
The great wind blows toward Vāyu; this is the illustration.

A *repha* becomes a *repha* when followed by *ś*, *ṣ*, or *ha*. One should observe that it occurs after *varṣo* and *arhāt*; however, one should not apply it in the case of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). 9–10.

Regarding the example "vvarṣman varṣyāyām antar-hṛdā," therein the letter *l* would also become similar to the letter *e* due to their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*). Furthermore, regarding the examples "śatabalśā" and "balhā," therein [the same principle applies].
Wherever there is an *anusvāra*, it invariably becomes *ṛ* or *ṭha*.
It is proclaimed to be of three kinds: short, long, and heavy.
A long vowel follows after a short one; such is the observation regarding *harṭhaḥ saḥ*. 12–13.
"A short vowel following a long one [is heavy] after words such as *māṃsa*"; this is the established view. For when a guru (long vowel) follows, the *anusvāra* is indeed considered to be heavy.
In the phrase *siṃhyasi*, that [vowel] before the *ṛkāra* is indeed long.
Likewise, it resides in the hearts of the gods and similarly in the mouths of thieves.
Now he speaks of the *ayogavāhas*: the *visarga* following the letter *a* and the vowel *ṛ* is purely guttural.

Likewise from the vowel *i*, and likewise from the vowel *u*, and that which is preceded by *e* (16), as well as that preceded by *au*, certainly becomes palatal (*tālavya*). And from *ai*, the visarga certainly becomes both guttural and palatal (*kaṇṭhatālu*). (17)
Likewise, from the letters *au* and *o*, which belong to the throat and the lips, the *visarga* certainly arises;
here, the god Savitṛ is like the letter *ha*.
The three goddesses are the *visarga*, and it is like the sound *hi*.
In "ākhuste paśuḥ" and similar cases, it becomes like the letter *ha*.
In "visargaścāgneḥ" and similar cases, the *visarga* becomes like the letter *he*.
In "visargo bāhvoḥ" and similar cases, the *visarga* becomes like the letter *ho*. (19–20)
Now, in cases such as *svairdṛkṣaiḥ*, the visarga becomes similar to the letter *hi*;
in cases such as *dyauṣpitā*, it becomes similar to the letter *ha*.
It is the established rule of the treatise that the [visarga] should not be considered as the letter *ha* at all. 21.
The *visarga* is certainly like the breath of a serpent (phaṇin). When there is a downward movement and a gathering (*pracaya*), the release from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*) occurs;
thus, "namas" belongs to Kūpya, as does the first and second [breaths] while one is awake. 22–23.
One should perform the "threatening gesture" (*tarjanī-mocana*) during an acute (*udātta*) vowel, but release [the finger] during an unvoiced (*visargaka*) one;

likewise, during a short (*hrasva*) vowel, the deity is Dharma, while during a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel, one should cast both. 24. In the case of an acute (*svāra*), the mortal horse becomes the target; in a long vowel, one should use the little finger.

When both [the preceding and following sounds] are short and the letter *va* is circumflex (*svarita*), and likewise when both are long, there is a "dropping" (*kṣepa*) [of the vowel]; such is the established rule of the scripture.
Just as [a crystal or a staff] may appear [otherwise] due to the influence of an external condition (*upādhi*).
In the same way, the *ūṣman* should be applied; "hihuheho" is the illustration, for "vvasoḥ pavitram" is cited there as the example.
Indeed, the ṛ-vowel everywhere becomes similar to the e-vowel.
"Hṛde," "mṛgaḥ," the third [verse], "ṛcam," "vācam," and then the next;
thus ends the Laghu-mādhyandinīya Śikṣā.
